questions.prompt: A large file is copied to a slow destination. What advantage does streaming provide over buffering it all first?

choices.text: A guarantee that each chunk is a complete logical CSV row.
A zero-memory guarantee independent of every chunk size.
Incremental processing without needing the whole file buffered up front.
A guarantee that the destination disk can never fail midway.

questions.explanation: Streams process pieces, avoiding whole-file buffering. They still have buffers, errors and format boundaries to manage.

questions.prompt: In source.pipe(destination), what roles normally apply?

choices.text: Both streams must buffer the complete payload before any chunk can move.
The source can disregard the destination buffer because pipe never uses backpressure.
The readable source supplies chunks; the writable destination consumes them.
The writable source supplies chunks; the readable destination consumes them.

questions.explanation: Readable and writable roles define data direction. Piping transfers incrementally and manages backpressure.

questions.prompt: destination.write(chunk) returns false. What should a manual producer normally do?

choices.text: Ignore it because only thrown exceptions can indicate backpressure.
Discard the current chunk because the internal buffer has lost it.
Stop producing more chunks until the destination emits drain.
Retry the same chunk immediately because false means it was rejected.

questions.explanation: The chunk was accepted into buffering; false signals to stop adding more until drain.

questions.prompt: What does drain signify for a writable stream that previously returned false?

choices.text: The source has ended and no more chunks may ever be written.
All pending chunks were rejected and must now be resent by the producer.
The buffer has drained enough that production can resume.
Every byte has reached permanent disk storage successfully.

questions.explanation: drain controls flow. It is not a durability acknowledgement or end-of-stream signal.

questions.prompt: Which API coordinates errors and cleanup across source, transform and destination?

choices.text: A source error listener alone, without handling destination or transform failure.
Promise.resolve(source.pipe(destination)), treating that resolved value as completion.
A write loop that ignores every stream error event.
pipeline, with a callback or Promise handling its completion.

questions.explanation: pipeline coordinates connected streams and propagates failures; its completion path must be handled.

questions.prompt: A writable highWaterMark is set to 16 KB. Which interpretation is accurate?

choices.text: It guarantees process resident memory never exceeds 16 KB.
It means the stream sends exactly one 16 KB packet per write.
It truncates every accepted chunk longer than 16 KB automatically.
It is a buffering threshold used to apply backpressure.

questions.explanation: The threshold indicates buffering pressure, not a strict allocation cap or network packet size.

questions.prompt: Which claims describe stream processing correctly? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Readable streams provide data that writable streams consume.
A transform stream can consume input and produce transformed output.
Chunks permit incremental processing of a large payload.
Streaming eliminates the need to handle errors from the destination.
Each chunk is guaranteed to align with an application record boundary.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: these are the respective stream roles. B: Correct: transforms expose writable and readable sides. C: Correct: whole payload buffering is unnecessary. D: Incorrect: I/O errors remain possible. E: Incorrect: chunking is not record framing.

questions.prompt: Which actions correctly respond to write returning false? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Pause further production until drain.
Keep listening for errors while waiting to resume.
Assume a thrown error must occur before backpressure can be meaningful.
Send the same chunk again immediately because it was not accepted.
Continue writing every remaining chunk regardless of the return value.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: wait for the writable flow signal. B: Correct: a flow pause does not prevent failures. C: Incorrect: false is the ordinary backpressure signal. D: Incorrect: write already accepted or queued that chunk. E: Incorrect: ignoring it can grow buffers unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Which pipeline properties matter for a file-export endpoint? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Pipeline coordinates cleanup of participating streams on failure.
A pipeline Promise rejection should be observed and handled.
Pipeline makes destination failures impossible after the first chunk.
Awaiting the pipeline Promise means no error handler is needed if it rejects.
Pipeline propagates stream failures through its completion callback or Promise.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: error handling includes stream destruction. B: Correct: observe success or failure explicitly. C: Incorrect: destinations can fail midstream. D: Incorrect: awaiting a rejected pipeline still requires normal error handling. E: Correct: its completion path reports failure.

questions.prompt: Which highWaterMark claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: In object mode it counts buffered objects rather than byte size.
It is a threshold for stream buffering and backpressure.
A chunk can push buffering beyond the threshold.
It guarantees every write exactly equals the specified buffer size.
It is always a global hard limit on all process memory.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: units differ for object mode. B: Correct: it drives flow-control decisions. C: Correct: a threshold is not a strict ceiling. D: Incorrect: callers can write differently sized chunks. E: Incorrect: other buffers and allocations exist.
